summary: This experimental document introduces Model-Based Metrics, a way to judge whether an Internet path can be expected to meet a target transport performance for bulk data. It does this by running diagnostic tests on successive subpaths rather than on the whole path at once. The approach tests the network against a model of how a transport protocol should behave.

plainLanguage.summary: To check whether a long road is fast enough, you test it one short piece at a time. This does that for internet paths carrying big downloads.

questions: how to test if a path supports a target throughput
what is a targeted ip diagnostic suite
subtitle: Judging an Internet path by testing it one piece at a time against a model of how TCP needs to behave.

tldr.problem: Measuring bulk transfer capacity with TCP itself gives results that depend on the test path, the vantage point and TCP's own congestion, so they do not predict what users will see elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: From a target data rate, round-trip time and MTU, mathematical TCP models give a window size and a required run length between losses. A suite of open-loop IP tests sends precomputed bursts across each subpath and checks loss and marking statistics against those criteria.
tldr.outcome: A subpath passes only if all tests pass, giving a pass, fail or inconclusive answer that different parties can repeat. The RFC is Experimental and only a framework, not a full test specification.

facts.label: Bufferbloat rule of thumb
facts.value: Loss before queuing delay exceeds 2x target RTT

today: RFC 8337 is an Experimental specification, published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation. It is a modeling framework rather than a complete test specification, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why TCP Makes a Poor Measuring Tool
sections.content:
Bulk Transport Capacity (BTC) is a path's ability to carry bulk data such as large files and non-real-time streaming video. The RFC explains why measuring it has been so hard. TCP is a control system with circular dependencies, so everything affects performance. Congestion control finds a dynamic equilibrium, raising the rate until the network drops packets or adds ECN CE marks, so the losses it sees are mostly set by TCP itself. TCP's ability to compensate for impairments is inversely proportional to RTT, so an impaired subpath can pass a short-RTT local test and fail on a longer path.

Measurement traffic and cross traffic also interact in unknown ways, and two independent TCP implementations rarely produce the same result under identical conditions.

Model-Based Metrics (MBM) avoid this by making the measurement open loop: the traffic pattern is computed from the target and does not change in response to what the network does. The goal is metrics an ISP can act on, that compose across subpaths, that give the same result from different vantage points, and that multiple parties can repeat.
sections.plainLanguage: If you race a runner to see how fast a track is, the runner's own tiredness gets in the way. So instead you measure the track piece by piece with a fixed plan that does not change as you go.

sections.title: The Modeling Framework
sections.content:
The starting point is a Target Transport Performance made of three values: the Target Data Rate, the Target RTT (the longest baseline round-trip time the user expects to cover) and the Target MTU (assumed to be 1500 bytes unless stated). Mathematical models turn these into traffic parameters and statistical criteria. Together they define a Targeted IP Diagnostic Suite (TIDS). A Fully Specified TIDS (FSTIDS) adds details the RFC leaves out, such as packet type and vantage selection.

Two numbers drive most tests. The target window size is the average packets in flight needed to hit the rate, computed as ceiling(target_rate * target_RTT / (target_MTU - header_overhead)). The reference run length, the minimum packets delivered between losses or ECN CE marks, is 3*(target_window_size^2). That comes from a deliberately conservative Reno-style AIMD model with delayed ACKs. Alternate models and derating are allowed if the FSTIDS documents and validates them.

The end-to-end loss budget is apportioned across subpaths, so likely bottlenecks may use more of it and others must use less. A subpath passes if and only if every test passes. The framework assumes a Reno-style, window-controlled transport that responds to loss and ECN marks.
sections.plainLanguage: You decide how fast the trip needs to be, then do some math to learn how many cars must be on the road and how few accidents are allowed. Each piece of the road gets a share of the allowed accidents.

sections.title: Test Streams That Mimic TCP
sections.content:
The test streams copy the way TCP sends data in bursts. In slowstart, efficiency features such as TCP Segmentation Offload and delayed ACK produce a two-level pattern: small bursts at the sender's interface rate (typically 3 or 4 packets), grouped into a larger slowstart burst sized from the window and repeated once per RTT. The RFC assumes four-packet bursts and a slowstart rate of twice the implied bottleneck capacity.

Rate can be controlled in several ways. Paced bursts are sent on a timer. A Constant Window Pseudo CBR test runs a self-clocked protocol with a fixed window. A Scanned Window test raises the window by one packet for every 2*target_window_size packets delivered, imitating Reno's additive increase to find the onset of queuing and of loss. A stiffened transport that ignores loss would violate mandatory congestion control and is only for laboratory use.

Most details are deterministic and precomputed, so the test does not depend on measurement points. The procedures apply to a single stream. Multiple flows are discouraged for rates below several megabits per second, and are acceptable only if the TIDS says so.
sections.plainLanguage: The test copies the way a real download behaves: little handfuls of packets, then bigger waves, then waves that keep growing. That way the road gets the same kind of surprise a real download would give it.

sections.title: Interpreting Results and Statistics
sections.content:
Every test ends as pass, fail or inconclusive. A test is inconclusive when the traffic pattern was not generated accurately, the result is not statistically significant, or the preconditions were not met. If all tests pass but some are inconclusive, the whole suite is inconclusive.

Loss and mark counts are judged with a Sequential Probability Ratio Test. The null hypothesis H0 is no more than one mark in target_run_length packets, and the alternative H1 is one or more marks in target_run_length/4 packets, with example error levels of 0.05. Testing continues until one hypothesis can be accepted.

All tests must also record packet reordering. As a strawman, transports should tolerate a reordering extent of up to the larger of one quarter window or 1 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: You keep counting how many packets get lost. Once you have counted enough to be sure the road is fine, or sure it is not, you stop. If you cannot be sure, the answer is 'can't tell'.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Tests
sections.content:
The tests come in groups. Basic data rate and packet transfer tests check delivery statistics at the target rate, paced or window-controlled, plus a low-rate background test for ongoing monitoring. Standing queue tests are engineering tests that scan across the onset of queuing and loss. They check that the first loss comes after more than target_run_length packets, that loss starts before queuing delay exceeds twice the target RTT (a rule of thumb against bufferbloat), that loss is not excessive, and that a half-duplex link does not fall back to stop-and-wait.

Slowstart tests send bursts of target_window_size packets at the slowstart rate to check the bottleneck queue, plus an AQM test. Sender rate burst tests check that the network can absorb full-window bursts at the sender interface rate, for example after an application pause. This is the only test where derating is encouraged.

The Sustained Full-Rate Bursts test combines the capacity checks: send target_window_size bursts at interface rate every target_RTT and verify the run length. Passive measurement of constrained applications is also possible.
sections.plainLanguage: There are tests for each kind of trouble: is the road wide enough, is there a waiting area big enough for a sudden crowd, and does it tell cars to slow down at the right moment, not too early and not too late?

sections.title: Worked Example and Validation
sections.content:
The RFC's example targets minimal 720p HD video: 2.5 Mb/s, a 50 ms target RTT, a 1500-byte MTU and 64 bytes of header overhead. That gives a target window of 11 packets and a target run length of 363 packets. The simplest suite sends 11-packet bursts every 50 ms and allows at most 1 loss per 33 bursts (363 packets in 1.650 seconds).

The loss budget can then be split across subpaths: for example 50% to the access link, 40% to interconnections and 1% to each of up to 10 internal hops. An interconnect with 40% would allow fewer than one loss per 82 bursts (902 packets). The RFC contrasts this with unconstrained TCP tools, which on very short RTTs tend to report inflated rates.

Because the models are conservative and may be derated, the RFC asks for validation. Publish the suite openly, and show that real applications meet the target on a testbed built so every test passes only by a small margin. The procedures are described as still experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: For a video that needs a steady stream, the math says to send a little crowd of 11 packets every 50 milliseconds and allow almost no losses. Each part of the road is told how many losses it is allowed to cause.

viz.caption: WHAT MODEL-BASED METRICS ARE MEANT TO PROVIDE

items.title: Actionable
items.text: Results map to IP-layer behavior an ISP can test, repair and verify.

items.title: Composable
items.text: Measures of joined paths should be predictable from the subpaths.

items.title: Vantage invariant
items.text: The result holds across a wide range of measurement point choices.

items.title: Repeatable
items.text: A consumer and an ISP can run the same measurement and get the same result.
